US.why: Near horizons held, ten-year anchor held. The rate shock peaked and the market held. The S&P fell on 7 and 8 Oct as the 10-year touched 5.365%, its highest since April 2002, then rallied 0.59% to 7811.54 on 9 Oct, just under its record close of 7818.93 set on the 6th. The 10-year auction cleared at 5.3%, the highest since November 2000, but with indirect bidders taking 80.3% - demand for duration at these yields is there. The September minutes had most participants seeing another hike by year-end; CME FedWatch had October at 21.6% and December at 86.2% on 6 Oct. The consumer is the weak point: Michigan sentiment fell to 46.3 in October's first read, near May's record low of 44.8, with five-year inflation expectations up to 3.5%. September CPI on 14 Oct carries a 3.7% consensus. Hurricane Isaias shut in more than 70% of Gulf crude output. Near horizons stay where the rate repricing put them. The anchor holds at 6.5 on two structural points: the US is a net energy EXPORTER, a relative tailwind against every other bloc here with Brent at $104.72, and NDX at 22.4x forward on its last verified reading sat below its 10y and 5y averages.
US.summary: Near horizons held: the S&P ended the week at 7811.54 near its record after the 10-year touched 5.365%; the anchor holds at 6.5 on energy self-sufficiency.

EUROPE.why: 3M CUT a quarter point to 2.25: a fiscal stress has joined the energy one. The 10-year OAT-Bund spread reached about 140bp, a level last seen in the euro debt crisis, as France's 2026 deficit is now expected at 5.4% of GDP against a 5.0% target and its 2027 budget faces a large austerity gap before a presidential election; BusinessWorld cited European fiscal and political concerns for the week's risk-off. The policy/growth mismatch stands: the ECB hiked to 2.50% on 10 Sep into IMF growth of just 0.9%, explicitly because the energy shock will hold inflation above target. August HICP was 3.2% (final), and September's flash jumped to 3.8% against 3.6% expected, with energy at 18.8%. Europe is the largest net energy importer in the world, facing Brent +60.56% y/y; the final print on 16 Oct tests the ECB's word that its cycle is over. 6M and longer held: a spread at crisis levels is a near-term risk premium until it forces a policy answer. The offset is real - at 15.4x forward it is the cheapest large market here.
EUROPE.summary: 3M cut to 2.25: the French OAT-Bund spread reached about 140bp on top of an ECB hiking at 2.50% into 0.9% growth and 3.8% flash inflation.

ASIA.why: Near horizons held after last week's cut; the earnings engine delivered and the market sold it. Samsung's preliminary third-quarter operating profit was a record 107.4tn won on 8 Oct, ahead of a 106.1tn consensus, and TSMC's September revenue was 54.6% above a year earlier - the AI supply chain is still earning. Korea fell anyway: the KOSPI lost 2.62% to 6,625.93 on 8 Oct, from 6,803.90 the day before, a third straight decline on oil and US rate fears, and was shut on the 9th. The Nikkei closed at 69,030.92 on 9 Oct, -0.02%, after recovering most of an early fall as SoftBank slid on doubts over AI revenue. Oil is back against the region's importers - Brent $104.72 - though China resumed refined-fuel exports after its Golden Week halt and Saudi Aramco's November price to Asia is a six-year low. The BoJ is at 1.25% after its 18 Sep hike, the yen weaker on it at 156.86; the Tankan reached 24. Korea, Taiwan and Japan are all large net oil importers. The ten-year anchor stays at 7.5: 10.5x forward against consensus EPS growth of ~52% and ~28% is a two-decade-wide discount, and JPM LTCMA puts EM equity at 7.8%, the highest of any equity block.
ASIA.summary: Ranked first over ten years: Samsung's profit hit a record 107.4tn won and 10.5x forward stays cheap; near horizons held as the KOSPI fell 2.62%.

PHILIPPINES.why: Near horizons held after last week's cut; the peso made the test harder. It closed at a record-weak 62.90 on 8 Oct, past the 62.86 of 14 Sep, on risk-off and oil, then recovered to 62.801 on 9 Oct; the 62.925 intraday trough of 15 Sep is still the weakest it has traded. That is a 6.39% loss of purchasing power against the dollar this year. The PSEi fell to a 2026 low of 5610.39 on 8 Oct and recovered 1.61% to 5700.99 on 9 Oct. September inflation was 7.2%, core 4.7%; food 6.7%, transport 14.6%, and the poorest 30% of households saw 9.0%. The nominal carry is rising to meet it - the 5 Oct auction lifted 91-day bills to 5.667% and 364-day bills to 6.214% - and BSP, at 5.00%, meets on 22 Oct with a hike now expected. Against 7.2% every tenor's real yield is still below zero. Oil is a headwind again, Brent at $104.72, though China's resumed fuel exports ease the products squeeze. The 12-month and ten-year horizons stay neutral: a BSP that hikes restores the real carry. This sleeve's job - zero duration risk and high nominal carry - is unimpaired. Its purchasing power is not.
PHILIPPINES.summary: Near horizons held: the peso closed at a record 62.90 and the PSEi at a 2026 low of 5610.39 on 8 Oct, with inflation at 7.2% before BSP on 22 Oct.

drivers.name: Monetary policy & liquidity
drivers.note: HELD at 2.0. The minutes confirmed the stance and the long end tested it again. Released on 7 Oct, the September minutes showed every participant behind the hike and most judging another by year-end appropriate, with almost all seeing inflation risks to the upside - the 16 of 18 dot-plot participants who saw one more hike, in words. The same day the 10-year traded as high as 5.365%, above the 5 Oct peak of 5.349% and the highest since April 2002 - still short of that year's 5.379% - then eased after the 10-year auction cleared at 5.3%, the highest such auction yield since November 2000, with indirect bidders taking 80.3%. On official closes it went 5.31% on the 5th, 5.27% on the 6th, 5.28% on the 7th and 5.22% on the 8th; the 9th read 5.24% on the Treasury par curve, provisional until FRED confirms it. The 30-year reached 5.733% on 7 Oct, also its highest since 2002, and was 5.60% on Friday; the 2-year 4.789%. CME FedWatch still has October off the table at 21.6% on 6 Oct - from 17% after the payrolls and 73% on 23 Sep - and a hike by December at 86.2%, from 66.2%. Held, not cut: the minutes said what the dots had, and yields ended the week below their peak. The ECB finished its cycle on 10 Sep at 2.50%; BSP is at 5.00% and meets on 22 Oct with the peso at a record low; the BoJ joined on 18 Sep at 1.25%.
drivers.summary: Held at 2.0: the minutes backed another hike by year-end, and the 10-year touched 5.365% on 7 Oct, a 2002 high, before a 5.3% auction cleared well.

drivers.name: Inflation trajectory
drivers.note: HELD at 2.5, with the test dated. No new print this week, but every expectation measure moved the wrong way. Michigan's October survey put year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.7% from 4.6% and five-year expectations at 3.5% from 3.4% - the long horizon is the one a central bank cannot ignore. Oil turned back up: Brent settled at $104.72 on 9 Oct, from $100.58 on 6 Oct, +60.56% on a year earlier against $65.22. September CPI is due on 14 Oct with a 3.7% headline consensus, from 3.4% in August; that print decides whether this score moves. The rest of the picture stands from last week: Philippine inflation 7.2% with core 4.7%, US services prices at 74.0, the euro-area flash at 3.8% with energy at 18.8%. Held, not cut: expectations surveys lead prints but are not prints, and US core was 2.4% in August.
drivers.summary: Held at 2.5: five-year inflation expectations rose to 3.5% and Brent climbed back to $104.72; September CPI on 14 Oct is the test.

drivers.name: Growth momentum
drivers.note: HELD at 4.0. The consumer is weakening; the activity data are not. Michigan sentiment fell to 46.3 in October's first read, from 48.1 and below the 48.0 expected, close to May's record low of 44.8, after the Conference Board's 81.9 in September. Hurricane Isaias shut in more than 70% of US Gulf crude output by 9 Oct - a supply shock with a weeks-long horizon, not a demand one. Against that, the ISM services index was 54.9 and manufacturing 54.5 in September, both inside expansion, and Japan's Tankan for large manufacturers reached 24, an eight-year high. September payrolls (+29k, unemployment 4.2%) already took the September raise back on 3 Oct. This driver's lane is whether the growth engine is intact under the shocks; sentiment at a record low with spending data still in expansion is a warning, not yet a break.
drivers.summary: Held at 4.0: Michigan sentiment fell to 46.3, near its record low, but services at 54.9 and manufacturing at 54.5 are still expanding.

drivers.name: Corporate earnings
drivers.note: Still the strongest pillar, and the quarter's first big number confirmed it. Samsung's preliminary third-quarter operating profit was 107.4tn won on 8 Oct, the first quarter above 100tn and ahead of a 106.1tn consensus, on memory; TSMC's September revenue was up 54.6% on a year earlier. Asia ex-Japan EPS of ~+52% (2026) and ~+28% (2027) stands. The market sold the news anyway - the KOSPI fell 2.62% to 6,625.93 on 8 Oct, a third straight loss, and SoftBank slid on doubts about AI revenue on the 9th - which is a positioning and multiple question, not an earnings one. Held, not raised: the beat was narrow against consensus, and Brent back at $104.72 squeezes the margins of the region's manufacturers. US third-quarter results begin with the banks on 13 Oct.
drivers.summary: Still the strongest pillar: Samsung's Q3 profit hit a record 107.4tn won and TSMC's September sales rose 54.6%, though chips sold off.

drivers.name: Valuation support
drivers.note: HELD at 8.0 after last week's cut. The S&P closed at 7811.54 on 9 Oct, just under its record close of 7818.93 on 6 Oct, after two down days on the yield spike: the market neither re-rated further nor gave the discount back. NDX at 22.4x forward on its last verified reading sat below its 10y (22.9x) and 5y (24.7x) averages; Asia at 10.5x is a two-decade-wide discount, with the Nikkei at 69,030.92; Europe is at 15.4x. A cheaper multiple on the same earnings is better compensation for the same risk, and this week the multiple did not move.
drivers.summary: Held at 8.0: the S&P ended the week at 7811.54, just under its 7818.93 record, neither re-rating further nor giving the discount back.

drivers.name: Volatility & risk appetite
drivers.note: HELD at 3.0, and the curve under it corrected. The index rose 0.47% to 15.08 on 7 Oct and 2.19% to 15.41 on 8 Oct as the 10-year hit its 2002 high, then fell 3.70% to 14.84 on 9 Oct as stocks rallied - a low level, under the 17.84 close of 10 Sep and below the long-run 19.5, so it reads as neither complacency nor stress. THE CURVE WAS WRONG FOR ITS DATE. The strip carried since 3 Oct (October 18.65 to January 20.38, labelled 2 Oct) read 4.16% high against the published VIX3M of 17.72 on 7 Oct; it had matched only the 1 Oct VIX3M, the one reading the check then had, dated a day before the strip. Re-quoted to the 5 Oct Cboe settlements (October 17.46 to January 19.33), the curve reads 17.57 against that 17.72, -0.87%. What this driver does NOT carry is a claim that rising volatility pays the portfolio: every fund's base return already assumes long-run volatility, so only the curve's distance from 19.5 moves a forecast. Blended across horizons the re-quoted curve sits at 18.97.
drivers.summary: Held at 3.0: the VIX ended at 14.84; the curve was re-quoted after the old strip read 4.16% high against VIX3M, and now blends to 18.97.

drivers.name: Geopolitics & energy
drivers.note: HELD at 1.75 for a third week, on two facts pulling opposite ways. The security leg worsened again: Reuters counted at least 12 tankers attacked in the week to 5 Oct, the most intense week of the war, and the attacks spread inside the Gulf - a chemical tanker hit off Qatar with crew casualties on 7 Oct, another set on fire east of Fujairah on 8 Oct. UKMTO had logged nine attacks in October by the 6th, against 18 in all of September. Brent settled at $104.28 on 8 Oct and $104.72 on 9 Oct, from $100.58 on 6 Oct, with Hurricane Isaias shutting in more than 70% of US Gulf output on top. The escalation tail narrowed: on 8 Oct the President said the US would not strike Iran before the 3 November midterms, after The Atlantic reported the White House had asked for strike options, and on 9 Oct he called talks 'productive', where Iran's president had called them 'meaningless' on the 6th. The energy leg still holds on VOLUME, the measure this note says to read: Goldman had Gulf oil exports, dark flows included, at 23.3 mb/d over the week to 29 Sep, above the 23.0 pre-war level its 28 Aug note implied when it read 15.5; JPMorgan had Middle East crude at 17.5 mb/d, 98% of pre-war, products 58%. On 22 Sep Saudi Arabia restarted the 1200 km East-West pipeline, which ran at 5.8 mb/d on 6 Oct; Saudi Aramco cut November Arab Light to Asia to $5 below the benchmark from $2 below, and the G7 plans a 100-million-barrel release. Held, not cut: ships are being hit inside the Gulf, but the one escalation that could close it - a US strike - is off the table until 3 Nov. The queue off berth read 206 vessels on 7 Oct, inside a 147-443 range. Read the disruption on VOLUME, not vessel counts: IMF PortWatch counted 4 transits on 4 Oct against an 85 baseline, a 95% drop; Lloyd's List Intelligence 14 a day in the week to 23 Aug counting only cargo over 10000 dwt; the US government around 30 on a basis it does not state - and none of them is supply. Still close to the floor of 1: the stress table's full closure with Brent above $130 is a strictly worse state still on the table.
drivers.summary: Held at 1.75: tanker attacks spread inside the Gulf and Brent rose to $104.72, but a US strike is off the table until the 3 November midterms.

funds.name: ATRAM Peso Money Market Fund
funds.target: Own mandate: outperform PH bank deposits, average portfolio duration <= 1 year
funds.gross_note: 10y average PH short-rate path. Anchored on the PH bill curve - 91d 5.667%, 182d 5.971%, 364d 6.214% at the 5 Oct auction, higher across the curve than when this assumption was set on 2 Sep - with BSP at 5.00% after a third consecutive hike, reverting toward a ~4.50% neutral policy rate by year 3-5. Held at 4.85% and flagged rather than re-fitted: the rise sits in the part of the path that reverts within a few years, which lifts a ten-year average by roughly a tenth of a point - inside this assumption's precision, but a known upward bias until it is re-fitted. CUT from 5.25% when the mandate lengthened to 10 years: the elevated front end is a 1-3 year feature, so over a decade far more of the path sits at neutral and the average falls toward it.
funds.dd_k_why: Not applicable - the cash sleeve is floored by a rate shock, not by the equity formula.

funds.fee_note: 1.50% ATRAM management fee + 0.35% target-fund TER (both verified)
funds.gross_note: NDX long-run total return of 8.0% (JPM LTCMA US large cap 6.7% + 1.3% NDX growth premium, valuation neutral at 22.4x vs 22.9x 10y avg), times ~78% covered-call upside capture, plus ~0.5%/yr of option premium at long-run implied vol.
funds.dd_k_why: At the 1.65 anchor: the premium's cushion is already in this sleeve's volatility (0.681x the Nasdaq-100) and its return; capped upside with full downside is negatively skewed, which argues against a lower k, not for one.

funds.gross_note: US large cap 6.7% (JPM LTCMA) + 3.5% tech earnings-growth premium - 1.2% multiple de-rating drag. Deliberately well BELOW the target fund's realised 15.20% 5y, which was earned inside an AI capex boom and is not a forecast.

catalysts.why: The test the inflation driver is held for. Consensus is 3.7%, from 3.4% in August, with Brent back at $104.72 and five-year inflation expectations up to 3.5%. It is the last CPI before the 28 Oct FOMC.
The flash said 3.8%, from 3.2%, with energy at 18.8% - above the 3.6% expected. A final at or above it tests the ECB's word that its cycle ended at 2.50% on 10 Sep, and the Europe ranking with it.

BSP is at 5.00% after three hikes, the last on 27 Aug. September inflation printed 7.2%, core 4.7%, and the peso closed at a record 62.90 on 8 Oct: a hike lifts the peso sleeve's carry toward a positive real yield, a pause leaves it deeper below zero.

FedWatch has October at 21.6% and a hike by December at 86.2% (6 Oct), after 29k September payrolls took October off the table on 2 Oct. The minutes had most participants seeing another hike by year-end, so the question is when.

The date both sides of the Hormuz talks are working to. Iranian officials have said a deal is unlikely before it. On 8 Oct the President said the US would not strike Iran before it - and has called renewed strikes after it 'possible'. The stress table's full closure is the state this date can bring back.

postponed.what: Iran-GCC talks on the Strait, in Oman
postponed.why: Called off on 14 September with no new date; Iran was to unveil the temporary shipping lane agreed with Muscat. US and Iranian delegations met at the UN on 22 September instead, and that meeting is what restored the energy driver.

dd_model.note: 1.65 is the calibration anchor, not the coefficient every sleeve uses. Each fund carries a declared adjustment for the shape of its own left tail; the portfolio coefficient is the weighted average across the equity sleeves. The whole quantity is then scaled by sqrt(horizon / calibration window), because expected maximum drawdown grows with the square root of the horizon - the -20% and -33% anchors are rolling FIVE-year medians and cannot simply be relabelled for a longer mandate.
